paragraphs: Friend, Asaph shows us something big. When the worst happens, you don't have to dress it up before you bring it to God. Asaph says it plain: the nations have invaded, Jerusalem is rubble, and he asks, "How long, O LORD?" (Psalm 79:5). That's a man who believes God can hear the ugly stuff, and I LOVE that.

Look at where he turns in the middle. He asks God not to hold past sins against His people, and he asks for compassion to come quickly (Psalm 79:8). He asks God to "atone for our sins" and says why: "for the glory of Your name" (Psalm 79:9). He isn't leaning on how good his people have been. He's leaning on who God is, and that's the only ground that never cracks. I spent years in a drawer figuring that out, and I'm still a little embarrassed it took me so long.

And watch how Asaph ends. He doesn't stay in the rubble. He says God's people, "the sheep of Your pasture," will thank Him forever and declare His praise from generation to generation (Psalm 79:13). So here's the lesson, baker: bring God the groans, trust His name over your own record, and expect a day for thanks. A prayer that starts in ashes can still end in a song.
